questions.problem:
Suppose that a function $f(x,y,z)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}=(x{y}^{2}+2y){e}^{xy}+2{z}^{3},\,\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂z}=6x{z}^{2}.
$$

 

Evaluate the following expression at the point $(1,0,1):$

$$
\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

Hence, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x} & =\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂y∂{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((x{y}^{2}+2y){e}^{xy}+2{z}^{3}) \\  & =(x{y}^{2}+2y)\cdot x{e}^{xy}+(2xy+2)\cdot {e}^{xy}+0 \\  & =({x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4xy+2){e}^{xy}.\end{aligned}
$$

In addition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂z}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(6x{z}^{2}) \\  & =12xz.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate both partial derivatives at the point $(1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}{|}_{(1,0,1)} & =(0+0+2){e}^{0}=2 \\ \frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,0,1)} & =12(1)(1)=12\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}{|}_{(1,0,1)}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,0,1)} & =2+12=14.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

I. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡x$

II. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=y{e}^{xy}$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=x{e}^{xy}$

III. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=2y+1$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=2y+1$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{xy}) \\  & ={e}^{xy}+xy{e}^{xy} \\  & ={e}^{xy}(1+xy) \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{xy}) \\  & ={e}^{xy}+xy{e}^{xy} \\  & ={e}^{xy}(1+xy).\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y+1)=2 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y+1)=0\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$,  the third pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II only'.

questions.problem: Given that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ evaluate ${f}_{yxy}(1,\frac{\pi }{2})$ if ${f}_{yy}(x,y)=-{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy).$
questions.worked_solution:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yxy}(x,y) & ={f}_{yyx}(x,y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{yy}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)) \\  & =-2x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+(-{x}^{2})\cdot (-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)) \\  & =-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+{x}^{2}y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
{f}_{yxy}(1,\frac{\pi }{2})=-2(1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})+(1)^{2}\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(1\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})=\frac{\pi }{2}\,\,
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

I. ${f}_{x}(x,y)={e}^{-2x}-y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)={e}^{-y}-2x$

II. ${f}_{x}(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=5$

III. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=2{y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡xy+{y}^{2}$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡xy+2xy\operatorname{cos}⁡xy+2xy$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{-2x}-y)=-1 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{-y}-2x)=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)=0 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡xy+{y}^{2})=4y\operatorname{cos}⁡xy-2x{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡xy+2y \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡xy+2xy\operatorname{cos}⁡xy+2xy) \\  & =2y\operatorname{cos}⁡xy+2y\operatorname{cos}⁡xy-2x{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡xy+2y \\  & =4y\operatorname{cos}⁡xy-2x{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡xy+2y.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$,  the third pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II and III only'.

questions.problem:
Evaluate ${f}_{zxz}(2,\frac{1}{2},1)$ given that a function $f(x,y,z)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

$$
{f}_{zz}(x,y,z)=2z\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2y)+x{e}^{z-2y}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{zzx}(x,y,z) & ={f}_{zxz}(x,y,z) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{zz}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2z\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2y)+x{e}^{z-2y}) \\  & =2z\cdot \frac{1}{x-2y}+{e}^{z-2y} \\  & =\frac{2z}{x-2y}+{e}^{z-2y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point  $(2,\frac{1}{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{zxz}(2,\frac{1}{2},1) & =\frac{2\cdot 1}{2-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}}+{e}^{1-2\cdot 1/2} \\  & =\frac{2}{2-1}+{e}^{1-1} \\  & =2+1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$
